reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because the speaker promotes StrongBlock nodes as a route to passive income and instructs viewers to buy ETH and obtain STRONG through a wallet and Uniswap, alongside a create-node call to action. The pitch uses a time-limited affordability message, suggests putting stimulus money into StrongBlock, and presents daily rewards and compounding node acquisition, while actual returns and individual eligibility are not established.

So we need to buy at least $900 of ETH. Make sure you have it in ETH and that's gonna be in your Metamask or a ledger and then you go to uniswap i'll put the link below and then you would purchase uh whatever the amount is to equal 10 strong
And this node is able to create passive income that allows you to acquire 0.2 strong per day per node
And there's a fee for running this node is 1495 Per month you have to pay out for maintenance on this node
one node will accumulate 0.2 strong per day so if you multiply that out it's going to take 50 days to accumulate 10 strong in rewards

opening.argument: The presentation includes material uncertainty and directs viewers to investigate for themselves, which is inconsistent with presenting the opportunity as a settled or guaranteed outcome. The speaker expressly says the reward target is adjusted and “not guaranteed,” identifies a recurring maintenance fee, and tells viewers that independent research is crucial, including checking the website and holder information. The discussion therefore presents a conditional market view with disclosed costs and risks, rather than an unconditional promise of profit.

citations.quote: The new target is 0.2 strong per day. So adjusted based on many factors, not guaranteed.
And there's a fee for running this node is 1495 Per month you have to pay out for maintenance on this node
you can go ahead and do your own research. That's crucial with any project.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing account emphasizes selected promotional language but omits the explicit qualification that rewards are adjusted and not guaranteed. Its cited calculation describes a projection based on a stated target, while the same presentation identifies a monthly fee and urges independent checking. A time-sensitive opinion about affordability does not itself establish deception or a guaranteed return.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The qualification is narrow: it adjusts the target, but the presentation still tells viewers that a node can provide passive income and builds a compounding calculation from the daily figure. Research language does not neutralize the direct purchase instructions, and disclosure of a fee does not show that the proposed returns are attainable or adequate to cover it.

opening.argument: The video's central activity is an operational walkthrough of how a blockchain node service works and how its interfaces are used. It explains obtaining STRONG through available markets, setting up MetaMask or a Ledger, connecting to Uniswap, and then using the StrongBlock site to create a node. The speaker also explains node infrastructure, including how nodes support a blockchain and how the service lowers the technical barrier. Those are concrete educational and technology demonstrations; the speaker describes his own fifth node and gives viewers steps to understand the process, rather than presenting an independently verified certification of the service.

make sure you set up your meta mask there's plenty of help videos on how to do that

I just created my fifth node to create passive income

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing account treats the walkthrough's purchase steps as proof of solicitation, but explaining how a wallet, exchange, and node interface operate is also ordinary technical instruction. The video identifies the node as a way to support blockchain infrastructure and describes the creator's own activity. A tutorial can discuss possible rewards without establishing that viewers were promised a particular financial outcome.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling the steps a tutorial does not change what the tutorial instructs viewers to do: acquire enough tokens, fund a wallet with ETH, use Uniswap, and create a node. The speaker does not merely explain software mechanics; he expressly links the procedure to passive income and gives a recurring reward figure. Technical detail can make a solicitation more actionable, not less.

opening.argument: The material can be understood as discussion of an ordinary paid blockchain service with a disclosed entry requirement and maintenance charge. The speaker describes node-as-a-service as a way to support infrastructure, says participation requires 10 STRONG, and identifies a monthly maintenance fee. The supplied instructions show token purchases and interaction with a smart contract, but do not show credential collection, recruiting a downline, or a guaranteed return. The reward target is expressly conditional, so the evidence does not establish a concealed scam mechanism rather than a service whose economics require evaluation.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing account calls the instructions a scam mechanism, but its own evidence shows a described service with an entry contribution and maintenance fee, not a hidden deposit or downline scheme. The speaker identifies the activity as supporting the blockchain and expressly qualifies the reward target. The presence of a purchase path and a create-node button establishes commerce and access, not fraud.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A paid service can still be the vehicle for scam-like returns. Here the required contribution, ETH purchase, node creation, and recurring STRONG reward are presented together as passive income. Calling the fee maintenance and the activity infrastructure does not establish that the service can sustain the advertised reward, while the missing credentials or downline are irrelevant to a paid-node return model.
